newsitem.title: HONG KONG: FUND VIEW - Funds see little change in Hong Kong.
newsitem.headline: FUND VIEW - Funds see little change in Hong Kong.

text.p: For institutional investors, little will change when the clock strikes midnight on Monday in Hong Kong.
The return of the British colony to China after 156 years under British sovereignty is a momentous political event, but of little consequence for fund managers.

As with most investors in the territory, fund managers with holdings in Hong Kong have assessed the risk of the handover, they are happy with it, and they are here to stay in happy anticipation of bumper returns from their China exposure.

"We remain more confident rather than less of the Hong Kong market in the next few months. We believe the market looks pretty attractive from the point of view of the opportunities coming up with China," said Stewart Aldcroft, director of marketing for Templeton Franklin Investment Services.

Christopher Ryan, managing director at HSBC Asset Management, said future opportunities with China, a more stable property market and the expected removal of a long-held political discount bodes well for Hong Kong stocks long term.
"There will be a significant improvement in bottom line earnings from companies whose business involves China exposure," Ryan said.

"The political discount that Hong Kong has always traded at relative to most other markets will start to disappear as people become more confident in the management of the economy. There is a probability that more money will flow into the market."
For global emerging market investors, Hong Kong's future is widely perceived as secure, a survey said last week.

"Fund managers consider the future of Hong Kong as being safe in China's hands, with the market benefiting from China's economic development and need for foreign investment," consultancy Burson-Marsteller said.
The survey found that many investors viewed the transition as being merely a "rubber-stamping of an existing situation because of Hong Kong's gradual integration with China's economy."

But the Burson-Marsteller survey confirmed findings of a Reuters poll - that some short-term volatility is expected, particularly in red chips, Hong Kong-listed companies with financial backing from China.

"These shares are starting 'to look toppy' and a correction in their rating is impending," the Burson-Marsteller survey said. Increased activity in the property sector, which has fuelled the Hong Kong stock market for the past few months, was also considered to be unsustainable in the longer term.
Looking further forward, the survey found overall sentiment towards the market remained positive.

It was widely believed that China would do nothing to undermine Hong Kong's position as an equity market and would support the market as a conduit for international capital investment to fuel its own growth, the survey found.
"Only a small minority voiced concern over market transparency and corruption, and that the situation would deteriorate under Chinese rule," the survey said.
